title: An original Arduino-controlled anaerobic bioreactor packed with biochar as a porous filter media
author: Küçükağa, Facchin, et al.
materials: Temperature control system: Heating and temperature control system were designed to operate the bioreactor at the desired mesophilic temperature range (34–38 °C). The heating system consists of two elastic resistance pads placed on the wall of the bioreactor bottle, a thermocouple fixed to the liquid recirculation hose, and a digital thermostat that provides power to the resistances depending on the measured temperature value. The digital thermostat had a 0.1 °C level of sensitivity for adjusting the set temperature level. Each component of the heating system and its electrical circuit diagram is described in the Additional Information. Moreover, a folding thermal jacket (made by aluminum foil) was placed to cover the entire walls of the glass bottle for sustaining a constant and homogeneous distribution of temperature conditions in the packed-bed reactor (Fig. 5c).

steps.title: Prepare bottle and cap
steps.instruction: Use a standard 0.5 L laboratory glass bottle (Duran or Pyrex) upside‑down as the reactor body and fit it with the custom four‑ported silicone‑O‑ring cap; the cap provides ports for gas injection, gas sampling, liquid sampling/injection, and liquid recirculation.

steps.title: Establish gas‑tight connections
steps.instruction: Connect all external equipment with quick‑connect pneumatic adapters; use laminated hoses made of an aluminum foil layer wrapped around PA12 polyamide tubing and sealed with silicone. Fit the multilayer hose to the submersible pump, apply a silicone seal over the joint, run the system with water overnight to leach any acetate from the silicone paste, then discard the wash water.

steps.title: Install heating and temperature control
steps.instruction: Attach two elastic resistance heating pads to the outer wall of the glass bottle, place a thermocouple on the liquid recirculation hose, and connect both to a digital thermostat with 0.1 °C resolution. Cover the bottle with a folding aluminum‑foil thermal jacket to ensure homogeneous temperature distribution. Set the desired mesophilic temperature (34–38 °C, typically 36 °C).

steps.title: Build digital gasometer
steps.instruction: Mount an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor on a 3‑D‑printed PLA holder and fix a Supel™ 30,226‑U 1 L flexible gas‑bag to the holder. Glue a rectangular rigid plastic piece on the top of the bag to improve ultrasound reflection. Connect the sensor to an Arduino Mega board that records distance readings and converts them to gas volume using the calibration curve.

steps.title: Assemble liquid recirculation system
steps.instruction: Connect a submersible mini pump (flow capacity 240 L h⁻¹, specified as 220 L h⁻¹ in the set‑up table) to the multilayer hose. Control the pump with an Arduino script that runs it in a regulatable pulsed mode. Build a sprinkling head from a modified plastic Pasteur pipette: cut off the needle tip, attach the filler to the hose with a cable tie, and drill a symmetric array of ≈2.0 mm holes using a hot soldering needle to obtain uniform liquid distribution without clogging.

steps.title: Prepare packing materials
steps.instruction: For the active (biochar‑packed) reactor, weigh 100 g wet biochar (69 % water), 325 g small glass beads (Ø 4 mm), and 200 g large glass beads (Ø 8 mm). For the control reactor, weigh 480 g large glass beads (Ø 8 mm). The net filter‑bed volume is ≈305 ± 15 mL; total liquid volume 200 mL; headspace ≈115 ± 15 mL.

steps.title: Load reactor and seal
steps.instruction: Keep the bottle vertical, insert the gas‑bag tube connector and the liquid recirculation tube (with the pipette head) into the central region of the bottle. Add packing layers in the following order for the active reactor: small beads, biochar grains, then large beads; for the control reactor add only large beads. Ensure tubes extend beyond the bottle so that, after sealing the four‑port cap, excess tube length remains for external connections. The cap ports have 6 mm ID and 18 mm OD; the restriction inside prevents media loss. Connect the liquid‑output tube as short as possible inside the cap to minimise dead volume, and insert the gas‑injection tube a few millimetres into the large‑bead layer. Seal the cap, turn the assembled unit upside‑down, fix it on a stable support, then attach the pump, digital gasometer, and thermal jacket.

steps.title: Calibrate digital gasometer
steps.instruction: Connect a 100 mL graduated syringe to the gas‑bag via a three‑way valve. Charge the bag in 50 mL increments up to 500 mL, recording the ultrasonic distance at each step; then discharge in the same 50 mL steps to zero. Repeat the full charge‑discharge cycle three times, average the distance values, and derive a linear correlation (≈25 mL mm⁻¹). Verify accuracy by introducing known volumes; the system shows ≈5 % error with a limit of detection of 9 mL.

steps.title: Perform gas leak tests
steps.instruction: Fill the reactor and gas‑bag with hydrogen (the most permeable gas) and monitor the gas volume for 2.5 h; a stable reading indicates no leak. Then fill the system with nitrogen, add water to the reactor, set the temperature to 36 °C, start liquid recirculation, and monitor overnight; a negligible change in total gas volume confirms impermeability.

steps.title: Start anaerobic fermentation
steps.instruction: Inoculate each reactor with anaerobic mixed‑microbial culture (MMC) from a digester treating grape pomace and sludge. Set the thermostat to 36 °C, start the Arduino‑controlled pulsed recirculation, and begin gas recording (Arduino reads ultrasonic sensor every 5 s). Feed glucose daily to achieve 20 g‑COD L⁻¹ in the liquid. Perform liquid sampling with disposable syringes through the quick‑connect liquid port placed before the pump; perform gas sampling with graduated syringes via the quick‑connect gas‑sampling port, first mixing headspace and gas‑bag contents with the syringe to homogenise the sample.

steps.title: Monitor COD and VFA
steps.instruction: Measure liquid COD with a Quick COD analyzer (ASTM D6238‑98). Determine gas COD by analysing daily gas volumes with a GC equipped with a thermal‑capture detector (TCD). Analyse volatile fatty acids in liquid samples using a GC‑MS with a DB‑FFAP polar column. Compile COD balances over the 10‑day test to assess reactor performance.
